message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"2.1","text":"On the following day, then, I, Clement, woke while it was still night and learned that Peter was awake and discussing piety with those who were with him (they were sixteen; and I resolved to give their names too, after learning each one’s name in due course, so that you may also know who they were: the first was Zacchaeus, the former tax collector, and Sophonias his brother; Joseph and his childhood companion Micaiah; also the twins Thomas and Eliezer; as well as the priests Aeneas and Lazarus; furthermore Elisha and Benjamin son of Saphra; likewise the builders Roubilos and Zechariah; the Iammeans Ananias and Haggai; and finally the companions Nicetas and Aquila). At any rate, I went in, greeted them, and sat down at his direction.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὡς ἑκάστου ἐξῆς χρόνου μαθών","chosen":"after learning each one’s name in due course","rationale":"The genitive ἑκάστου supplies the possessor of the previously mentioned “names,” while ἐξῆς χρόνου indicates their being learned successively over time."},{"source_quote":"ὁ τούτου σύντροφος Μιχαίας","chosen":"his childhood companion Micaiah","rationale":"σύντροφος denotes someone reared together with another and may alternatively be rendered “foster-brother” or “companion from youth.”"},{"source_quote":"οἱ ἰαμμηνοί","chosen":"the Iammeans","rationale":"The uncommon group designation is transliterated rather than silently identified with or emended to a better-known place-name."},{"source_quote":"προσαγορεύσας","chosen":"greeted them","rationale":"The verb here denotes addressing those present by way of greeting; the implied object is supplied from the surrounding company."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"οἱ ἰαμμηνοί","issue":"The printed ethnonym or group designation is uncommon, and its precise geographical identification is uncertain. The translation therefore preserves it by transliteration.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"2.2","text":"He, however, interrupted the discourse under way and, as though defending himself, fully explained why he had not awakened me so that I could listen to the discussion, giving as his reason the exhaustion caused by the voyage. Wanting that exhaustion to be soothed for me, he had allowed me to rest. “For whenever the soul is occupied with what the body lacks, it does not receive the lessons being offered as they deserve. For this reason, I do not wish to converse with those who are deeply grieved by some misfortune, excessively angry, carried away into a frenzy of desire, physically worn down, buffeted by the concerns of daily life, or troubled by any other passions—passions under which the soul, as I said, falls and, sharing the suffering body’s pain, also keeps its own understanding occupied.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸν ἐκ τοῦ πλοῦ σκυλμόν","chosen":"the exhaustion caused by the voyage","rationale":"σκυλμός can denote trouble, strain, or weariness; the voyage and subsequent need for rest favor physical exhaustion."},{"source_quote":"ἐκεῖνον πεφθῆναί μοι θέλων","chosen":"Wanting that exhaustion to be soothed for me","rationale":"πεφθῆναι is taken in the sense of being softened, assuaged, or worked off. “Overcome for me” is a more literal but less natural alternative."},{"source_quote":"περὶ τὸ λεῖπον τῷ σώματι ἀσχολῆται","chosen":"is occupied with what the body lacks","rationale":"The rendering preserves the supplied λεῖπον, referring to a bodily deficiency or unmet need rather than replacing it with a conjectural expression for bodily suffering."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς λύσσαν ἔρωτος ἐκτετραμμένοις","chosen":"carried away into a frenzy of desire","rationale":"ἔρως may denote erotic passion or intense desire, while λύσσα supplies the image of frenzy or madness."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ βιωτικῶν φροντίδων περιωθουμένοις","chosen":"buffeted by the concerns of daily life","rationale":"περιωθέω conveys being pushed or driven about, and βιωτικαὶ φροντίδες are concerns arising from ordinary worldly life."},{"source_quote":"οἷς ἡ ψυχὴ (ὡς ἔφην) ὑποπίπτουσα καὶ τῷ σώματι πάσχοντι συναλγοῦσα, καὶ τὴν αὐτῆς φρόνησιν ἀσχολεῖ.","chosen":"passions under which the soul, as I said, falls and, sharing the suffering body’s pain, also keeps its own understanding occupied","rationale":"The relative οἷς refers to the passions, while ὑποπίπτουσα and συναλγοῦσα are subordinate participles describing the soul. The finite predicate ἀσχολεῖ supplies the culminating assertion that the soul occupies its own understanding."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἐκεῖνον πεφθῆναί μοι θέλων","issue":"The compressed construction personifies the voyage-related exhaustion, and the exact nuance of πεφθῆναι is uncertain. Viable contextual senses include “be soothed,” “be worked off,” and “be overcome.”","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"2.3","text":"And let no one say, “Then comfort and admonition should not be offered to those who are doing something wrong.” I say, “If someone achieves a result, let him offer them; but if not, let him yield to the occasion.” For I know that “everything has its own time.” Therefore, words that strengthen the soul must be given to people before adversity, so that, if anything bad should ever come, the mind, armed beforehand with right reasoning, may be able to withstand what has been brought upon it. For then, at the height of the battle, the mind knows how to come to the aid of the one who has helped it through good counsel.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τοῖς φαῦλόν τι πράττουσιν","chosen":"those who are doing something wrong","rationale":"The accusative object with πράττουσιν indicates committing or doing something bad, rather than merely faring badly."},{"source_quote":"Εἰ μὲν ἀνύει τις","chosen":"If someone achieves a result","rationale":"ἀνύει is used absolutely for accomplishing something or producing an effect; the result of the offered counsel is implicit."},{"source_quote":"τῷ καιρῷ εἰξάτω","chosen":"let him yield to the occasion","rationale":"καιρός denotes the suitable or opportune time, and εἴκω means to give way or defer to it."},{"source_quote":"πρὸ τῆς κακώσεως","chosen":"before adversity","rationale":"κάκωσις can denote affliction, harm, or distress; “adversity” fits the subsequent image of something bad coming upon the mind."},{"source_quote":"παρὰ τὴν ἀκμὴν τοῦ πολέμου","chosen":"at the height of the battle","rationale":"ἀκμή denotes the culminating or most intense point. The phrase is attached here to the mind’s coming to aid; it could alternatively modify the earlier helping through good counsel."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ὁ νοῦς. προωπλισμένος","issue":"The printed full stop separates the subject ὁ νοῦς from the participle προωπλισμένος and the later verb δυνηθῇ, although they can form one continuous construction. The translation provisionally treats the stop as editorial punctuation rather than as evidence of omitted wording.","proposed_reading":"ὁ νοῦς προωπλισμένος","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"2.4","text":"“However, I have learned, Clement, that in Alexandria Barnabas thoroughly expounded to you the discourse about prophecy. Or did he not?” And I answered, “Yes, and very well.” Peter said, “Accordingly, it is not necessary to spend the present time, which can serve us for other teachings that you do not know, attending to those you do know.” And I said, “You are right, Peter. But grant me this, since I have resolved always to remain with you: continue to guide me through the discourse about the prophet, as I gladly listen. For without him, as I learned from Barnabas, it is impossible to learn the truth.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸν περὶ προφητείας λόγον","chosen":"the discourse about prophecy","rationale":"προφητεία denotes prophecy or the subject of prophetic revelation; the rendering does not replace it with the later and distinct phrase “about the prophet.”"},{"source_quote":"εἰς ἑτέρους λόγους οὓς οὐκ ἐπίστασαι","chosen":"for other teachings that you do not know","rationale":"λόγοι here refers to subjects of instruction or discourses rather than merely individual spoken words."},{"source_quote":"τὸν περὶ τοῦ προφήτου λόγον","chosen":"the discourse about the prophet","rationale":"The definite τοῦ προφήτου is retained without adding “true,” which is not present in the supplied Greek."},{"source_quote":"συνεχῶς ὑφηγεῖσθαι","chosen":"continue to guide me through","rationale":"ὑφηγεῖσθαι can mean to guide, instruct, or expound, while συνεχῶς gives the continuing character of the requested instruction."},{"source_quote":"ἄνευ γὰρ αὐτοῦ","chosen":"For without him","rationale":"The masculine pronoun is taken as referring to “the prophet,” which best fits learning the truth through him. Grammatically, reference to the masculine λόγος, “discourse,” remains possible, yielding “without it.”"}],"source_issues":[]}]}
